title: Barra's beach airport
hook: On the Scottish island of Barra, the plane lands on the beach when the tide is out.
peek: Barra, in the Outer Hebrides, has an airport whose runways are marked out on a sandy bay. It is the only place in the world where scheduled flights land on a beach, so the timetable is set by the tides.
lede: Barra Airport has no tarmac runway. Its three landing strips are laid out across Traigh Mhòr, a wide shell-sand bay at the north end of the island. Twice a day the sea covers them, so flights from Glasgow are timed for low tide. When the water is in, the runway is under the waves.

bullets.text: Wooden posts mark the ends of three strips arranged in a triangle, so pilots can choose the one that best faces the wind. Between flights the bay is an ordinary beach, and a windsock and flags warn walkers when a plane is due.
Loganair flies the route with Twin Otters, small sturdy planes built for short and rough strips. The flight from Glasgow takes about an hour and ends with a landing on firm wet sand.
Because the tide comes in about an hour later each day, the timetable shifts constantly. Bad weather or a very high tide can close the beach, so passengers learn to keep an eye on the sea.
The bay is famous for its cockles, and people still gather them on the sand between flights. The beach has served as both a larder and an airport since scheduled flights began in the 1930s.
